turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Gary, while we wait for the doctor, your blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-two and your pulse is seventy-six. The finger-prick just now is eleven point two.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Eleven point two? Is that dangerous, like right this minute? At home the fasting ones have been one-eighty-something, and I never write them down properly, I get flustered.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): One-eighty-something. Is that meter still on the American numbers?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. My brother posted it over from the States. Sometimes after tea it says two hundred and I just shut the book. I know that's hopeless.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I've seen the book. Half the squares are empty. When I'm there he scribbles something, but it's all over the shop.

[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): The GP referral has your night insulin as Lantus, twenty-two units. Tablets are metformin one gram by mouth twice a day, and Jardiance ten milligrams by mouth each morning.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty-two? No. I dial sixteen. I've been dialling sixteen for months. Did somebody change it and not tell me?
[SEG0008] person_3 (CAREGIVER): When I draw it up I set the pen on sixteen as well. I'm only in three mornings a week, mind, not at night.

[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hi Gary, I'm Doctor Shah. Nurse has left me the readings, blood pressure one thirty-eight over eighty-two, pulse seventy-six, sugar eleven point two. You've had type two diabetes for a while?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Eight years. Well, they found it when I was fifty-three, and I'm sixty-one, so yeah, eight years. Sorry, I'm a bit scrambled today.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's fine. What's been on your mind?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The sugars, and my feet. I keep picturing losing a toe. I do shifts at the warehouse in Dandenong, and on the earlies I skip the insulin. I get home, I eat, I'm knackered, and the pen stays in the fridge.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): You miss the night-time Lantus on the days you start early?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Maybe three nights, or four. Is that really bad? Just tell me straight.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Some weeks it's more than that. Last week he was on six earlies and I wasn't there to nag.

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I never took twenty-two. If the letter says twenty-two and I only dial sixteen, am I underdoing it? I can't go low on the forklift. We're not allowed to run it if we're hypo.

[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not changing any insulin number today, not while the referral says twenty-two and the two of you say sixteen. Have you actually had a hypo? Sweating, shaking, confusion?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No hypos. Not that I've noticed, and I'd notice, I think.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): The tablets are metformin, one gram by mouth twice a day with food, and empagliflozin, the Jardiance, ten milligrams by mouth every morning. Are those actually happening?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The metformin, yes, breakfast and with tea. The Jardiance, most mornings. If I'm rushing I forget that one, not as often as the insulin. Is forgetting it dangerous?
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): An odd missed tablet isn't ideal, but the missed insulin is the bigger hole. In your own words, what are the home sugars doing?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting, one-eighty-something, like I told the nurse. After tea, two-hundred-ish, sometimes. I don't trust my own writing. Does one-eighty mean I'm in strife?

[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's high, not a you're-about-to-collapse number. On that American meter one-eighty is roughly ten millimoles, and two hundred sits a bit over eleven, same sort of range as the eleven point two here. I'd like the meter and the book next visit so we stop guessing.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll bring them, I promise. What about the feet? They tingle at night, both of them, worse on the left, pins and needles. It wakes me up. Is that the diabetes eating the nerves?
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): High sugar can irritate nerves, but tingling on its own doesn't let me stamp that. Any sores, cracks, or numb patches you've found?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No sores. I mean, I don't think so.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I check his feet the mornings I'm in. Skin's not broken. He carries on like I'm tickling him.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): I've just had a look. The skin is intact, there's no ulcer, and both foot pulses are there. Soft touch is a bit dull on the left toes compared with the right.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Dull? So it is damage. Am I going to lose the foot? Please don't dress it up.

[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nothing I can see today says you're losing a foot. The night tingling and that dull patch make me think of early nerve irritation, possibly, not a definite diagnosis. What about the eyes, any blurring, floaters, trouble reading the roster?

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really any blurring. I had that photo screening about a year ago, maybe longer, and I can't remember the month at all. They said it was borderline, not quite the retina thing, but keep an eye on it. That was their word, borderline.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the letter called it borderline, and the date's fuzzy. Any change in the vision since then?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Vision's been the same. Am I going blind? Should I be booking the optometrist this week?

[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Borderline on a screening letter usually means they want it watched, not that you're going blind. I haven't seen that letter, so I won't invent a finding. If you get a sudden shower of floaters or a curtain across the vision, that's same-day, not a routine booking.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Also I'm thirsty all the time, and I'm up twice a night to wee. Is that just the sugar being high?
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thirst and getting up to pass urine fit with the sugars running high. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): The thirst, a few months. The weeing, um, well actually maybe since Christmas. I don't know. Call it a few months.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's been on about the thirst since February. I started buying the big bottles of water then.

[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me summarise, a few months is as close as we'll get on the thirst. Type two diabetes, about eight years. Metformin one gram twice a day and Jardiance ten milligrams each morning, both by mouth. Night-time Lantus is the messy bit: the referral says twenty-two units, you dial sixteen, and you skip it on the early shifts, several nights a week.

[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fasting readings at home are one-eighty-something, and they're not written down properly. The feet tingle at night, the skin is intact, and sensation is a bit dull on the left. The eye screening was called borderline, you can't date it, and the vision hasn't changed.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. That's the lot. So are you putting the insulin up? And can I still work? If I pass out on the forklift I'm done.

[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not putting it up today. Keep dialling the sixteen you've actually been using until your GP confirms the script, and please don't skip the work nights. If you feel sweaty, shaky or muddled, stop the forklift, check a sugar and take something sweet. You can keep working. You haven't been having hypos.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): What if sixteen is wrong and the sugars stay ugly? Is two weeks too long to wait? My mate takes metformin five hundred. Is one gram enormous?

[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): One gram twice a day is a standard full dose, not an overdose. Two weeks is alright if the insulin is going in and you know the hypo plan. If you have a hypo you can't sort yourself, or a sore opens on a foot, don't sit on it until you see me.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the Jardiance? A bloke at work said it gives you infections, you know, down below. Should I just stop it? I've been stewing on that for ages.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it because of a workmate. It can make genital thrush more likely. Have you had any itching or discharge?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I read stuff and I spiral, that's all.

[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Then it stays. If thrush turns up, ring the clinic and we treat it, it doesn't automatically mean the tablet goes. I'd like bloods today, an HbA1c, kidney function, and a urine albumin, so we're not flying on a muddled notebook.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Today? Do I have to be fasting? I had a coffee in the waiting room. Has that wrecked it?
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Coffee's fine. These don't need you fasting. Nurse can take them before you go. And the meter and the book come with you next time, not from memory.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can get the book here. I can't stand over him with the pen when I'm off, though. That's the hole.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fair. Gary, the work-night injection has to be yours. Phone alarm for when you walk in, pen out, sixteen units, then bed. Even if you're cooked.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll try. Honestly. The eye letter, do you chase it or do I?

[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll request the old report. If it doesn't show up, or it really does say borderline and they want a review, we'll book the eye clinic. Not this afternoon. You don't need to ring around today.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): And the tingling. Is there a tablet for that? I don't want a pile of new pills, but I don't want it getting worse either. Sorry. I know I'm firing questions.

[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): No new tablet today. If the tingling is from the sugars, getting those down comes first. If it's still waking you once the numbers are better, then we can talk about a nerve-pain medicine. That's a maybe, not a script.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): So when am I back?
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): Two weeks. Reception can book it on the way out. We'll have the bloods, the book, and hopefully a confirmed insulin dose, and then we decide if the number changes.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Okay. I'm still rattled, but you've said the foot isn't coming off today, so. Thanks.
[SEG0060] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll walk him to the desk. I might stick a bit of tape on the pen that says sixteen, so nobody gets clever with the dial.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tape's fine as a reminder of what he's actually dialling, not a new order. Nurse, can you take those bloods before he leaves?
[SEG0062] person_1 (NURSE): Yep, I'll do the HbA1c, the kidneys and the urine pot now. Gary, sleeve up when you're ready, it won't take long.

omissions.text: Lantus dose is recorded incompletely: the speakers said the GP referral lists insulin glargine (Lantus) 22 units nightly, but the patient has actually been dialling 16 units nightly for months and the doctor advised him to continue 16 units until the GP confirms the prescription.
Patient reports skipping the night-time Lantus on early-shift work nights, maybe 3 to 4 nights a week; caregiver says some weeks it is more, including last week with 6 early shifts.
Metformin timing detail was stated: patient takes it with breakfast and with tea/food.
Feet symptoms had additional key details: pins and needles, wakes him up at night.
Doctor asked about sores, cracks, or numb patches in the feet; only foot sores were recorded as denied. Cracks and numb patches were also specifically asked about and denied/not found by history.
Foot examination finding missing: foot skin was intact.

Eye history detail missing/wrongly simplified: prior diabetic eye photo screening was about a year ago or longer, and the patient said the letter/report said 'borderline, not quite the retina thing'; the doctor had not seen the letter and did not confirm an actual diagnosis.

Negative visual symptoms asked and answered incompletely: patient denied floaters/trouble reading by saying no vision change and vision has been the same; doctor specifically counselled urgent same-day review for sudden shower of floaters or curtain across vision.
Urinary symptom duration was more specific than recorded: nocturia may have been present since Christmas, though patient then approximated it as a few months.
The planned blood and urine tests were to be done today before leaving, and they do not require fasting; coffee was said to be fine.
